Verified directly against the Chamber of Deputies' own tramitacao record (dadosabertos.camara.leg.br, 76 recorded events): the Labour Committee approved the rapporteur's substitutive on September 15, 2025 -- which expanded the original cocoa-only text to all products -- the Economic Development Committee (CDE) approved its parecer on June 10, 2026, and the bill was received by the Constitution, Justice and Citizenship Committee (CCJC) on June 12, 2026, where it is awaiting designation of a rapporteur. Under the standing policy a formally tabled but unenacted import-ban bill is Partial, so the prior "No" was inconsistent with the classification rule rather than with the facts. Two dating corrections recorded: the CDE approval was June 10, 2026, not "the week of July 13" as this row previously stated, and the widely syndicated "committee approves" article is the Chamber's own September 15, 2025 story about the Labour Committee, not a 2026 item. Separately, Brazil's government (gov.br/Secom) called USTR's conclusion "regrettable," citing its ILO-recognised record; and a distinct, unrelated 25% Section 301 tariff (digital trade, ethanol, deforestation, IP) took effect July 22, 2026, on top of which the 12.5% forced-labour tariff was confirmed July 23, 2026. Summary and Source: Canada has had a forced-labor import prohibition since July 1, 2020 (Customs Tariff item 9897.00.00) but USTR flagged weak enforcement (only 2 shipments ever actually prohibited). A future run should not read that status label as progress. The Global Affairs Canada/CBSA consultation on forced-labour import identification criteria and importer evidentiary requirements, and a parallel ESDC supply-chain due-diligence consultation, remain open and CLOSED ON AUGUST 21, 2026 -- THE CLOSING DATE FELL ON THIS RUN. Summary and Source: President Abinader issued Decreto num. 502-26 on July 23, 2026 -- the day the 12.5% US tariff took effect -- establishing an administrative procedure empowering the Direccion General de Aduanas (DGA), coordinated with the Labor Ministry, Public Ministry, Industry and Commerce and Foreign Affairs, to identify, restrict and prohibit importation of merchandise produced wholly or partly with forced labor. The decree creates a public registry of prohibited products and lets DGA preventively retain or bar suspect goods including consignments already in transit or sitting at port, with re-export or destruction as remedies. DATE DISCREPANCY RESOLVED this run: at least one secondary outlet (Revista Mercado) dates the decree to June 23, 2026; the Presidency's own decree page for 502-26 carries 23 de Julio 2026, so the July 23 date recorded here is confirmed against the primary source and the June date is incorrect. The private sector has raised implementation concerns and commentators question enforcement capacity; no implementing regulation has been issued and no enforcement action has yet been identified. THIS IS NOW CONFIRMED FROM THE GOVERNMENT SIDE, THE FIRST GENUINELY NEW SUBSTANTIVE FINDING FOR THIS ROW IN WEEKS: Diario Libre of September 10, 2026, headlined "Aun no se aplican medidas contra el trabajo forzoso", which I fetched and read directly rather than taking from a summary, reports the Director General de Aduanas Nelson Arroyo saying the DGA cannot act until the Labour Ministry issues technical guidance -- "Hasta que el Ministerio de Trabajo no de las pautas tecnicas, nosotros no podemos tomar medidas". The classification is UNCHANGED at Yes -- the decree is enacted, and this tracker classifies on enactment, not on enforcement -- but this is an enforcement gap confirmed in the words of the official responsible for enforcing it, which is a stronger form of evidence than the commentator scepticism previously recorded here. THREE THINGS FOLLOW. First, it is explicitly a JULY SNAPSHOT, not a current roster, so my claim that a later-compiled list "had every opportunity" to include a 23 July decree was simply wrong. Second, "including" is hedged and the release nowhere claims the enumeration is exhaustive. Third, USTR publishes NO inclusion criteria and NO attendee roster, so there is nothing against which to test an operational-versus-enacted theory. The divergence is therefore an OPEN QUESTION, not evidence of anything, and the confident framing I gave it yesterday is withdrawn. What survives is narrower and still worth keeping: all twelve named economies are in this file's Yes column, which is real external corroboration, and three of this file's fifteen are unnamed. EL SALVADOR IS THE OMISSION THE SNAPSHOT DOES NOT EXPLAIN, and that is worth stating precisely rather than letting the correction sweep it away. The Article 27-A customs reform has been in force since around March 2026, comfortably inside any "by July 2026" cut-off, so unlike the Dominican and Vietnamese cases its absence cannot be attributed to compilation timing. Three possibilities remain open and none is established: the enumeration is non-exhaustive and El Salvador was simply not listed; USTR does not regard the Article 27-A reform as a measure "that prohibits the importation" in the relevant sense; or the list reflects something else entirely. Searches found no Salvadoran or US statement on the point and no Coexport reaction. Recorded as the sharpest open question arising from the release, and NOT acted on: this row rests on an enacted instrument and the standing policy classifies on enactment. Classification unchanged at Yes. SEARCHED PROPERLY ON SEPTEMBER 18 AND GENUINELY UNRESOLVED: a targeted hunt for any USTR, State Department, embassy or Salvadoran statement bearing on whether Article 27-A qualifies as a measure "that prohibits the importation" returned NOTHING, positive or negative. That is a gap in the available record rather than a research shortfall, and the question stays open. A NEW CONFUSABLE WAS CAUGHT IN THE PROCESS and is logged because it is unusually convincing: a USTR press release headlined "Ambassador Greer Issues Statement on Frameworks for Agreements on Reciprocal Trade with El Salvador, Argentina, Ecuador, and Guatemala" groups exactly the countries that would matter here and sits on ustr.gov. It is dated NOVEMBER 13, 2025 -- it predates the Salvadoran RTA signing of 29 January 2026 and the entire Section 301 action, and concerns framework announcements, not the forced-labour question. The country grouping makes it look far more relevant than it is. Rejected.

Summary and Source: USTR credits the EU with an enacted prohibition but assesses enforcement as inadequate because Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 is not applicable until December 14, 2027. Article 3 verified directly from EUR-Lex: "Economic operators shall not place or make available on the Union market products that are made with forced labour, nor shall they export such products." The Regulation is marked "(Text with EEA relevance)," the basis for Norway's incorporation, and Article 2(1) defines forced labour by reference to ILO Convention No. 29. The Commission's implementation guidelines of June 26, 2026 (C(2026) 4386 final) and the Forced Labour Single Portal are confirmed on the Commission's own initiative page, with implementation-readiness webinars scheduled from September 2026. SCHEDULE CONFIRMED this run: the Commission's programme opens in September 2026 with a general introduction to the Forced Labour Regulation and its preparedness package, followed by SME-focused guidance sessions and sector-specific sessions running through November 2026, including a dedicated TEXTILE-sector workshop on October 20, 2026. All of this is readiness support for a prohibition that still does not apply until December 14, 2027, so the classification is unaffected. NEW this run and verified directly against EUR-Lex: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/903 of 24 April 2026, adopted under Article 7(7)(a) of Reg. 2024/3015, specifies the details and functionalities of the information and communication system for the Regulation -- a dedicated forced-labour module within ICSMS (the market-surveillance system under Reg. (EU) 2019/1020), used for the general-provisions, investigations, decisions and enforcement chapters and for data exchange between the Commission, national competent authorities and customs. Its Article 11 provides that it enters into force on the twentieth day following publication in the Official Journal. THAT DATE IS NOW CONFIRMED FROM THE PRIMARY TEXT, retrieved directly from EUR-Lex this run: the implementing regulation is dated 24 April 2026 and its OJ citation is "OJ L, 2026/903, 27.4.2026," so the twentieth day following publication is 17 May 2026 -- which corroborates the date previously carried here only on secondary reporting. Its subject matter is also now stated precisely from the title: it specifies the details and functionalities of the information and communication system to be used for the purposes of Regulation (EU) 2024/3015. All of this is machinery for a still-inapplicable prohibition, so classification is unchanged. A NEAR-MISS WORTH RECORDING, September 12: a research pass's search synthesis initially described a "US-EU Framework Agreement of August 21, 2026" containing a forced-labour clause, which would have been a new bilateral instrument and material to this row. The pass checked it against the primary source titles before reporting it and found the Joint Statement is dated August 21, 2025 -- a year earlier, with terms effective September 1, 2025 -- and therefore predates and is superseded by the 2026 Section 301 action rather than being new. It was rejected before adoption. Logged because it is the same failure mode as the Peruvian expediente number and the Mexican March date: a plausible, specific, confidently stated fact that dissolves on contact with the source, and here the year was the only thing wrong with it. Source: EUR-Lex (primary texts of Reg. 2024/3015 and Implementing Reg. 2026/903); European Commission initiative 16292 and C(2026) 4386 final, June 26, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Regulation (EU) 2024/3015, Article 3 prohibition, in force but not applicable until December 14, 2027; Commission implementation guidelines adopted June 26, 2026, Forced Labour Single Portal live, and Implementing Reg. (EU) 2026/903 of 24 April 2026 establishing the ICSMS forced-labour module. SEPTEMBER 22 REFUTES A CLAIM THAT WAS FLAGGED BUT NEVER ADOPTED: a pass had reported, thin-coverage and explicitly unverified, that EU implementation guidelines were published in the Official Journal on 3 September 2026. They were not. The guidelines are C(2026) 4386 final, and the primary document was retrieved directly from the Commission at single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu (HTTP 200, 815,970 bytes, application/pdf) with its own internal links to eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/3015/oj/eng and to Commission initiative 16292. Its header reads "Brussels, 26.6.2026 C(2026) 4386 final" -- a Commission decision of 26 JUNE 2026, which is the date this row already carried, and a document of a kind not published as an L- or C-series act at all. So the 3 September date was a phantom, the row needed no change, and the value of the check was in stopping the claim rather than in changing anything. Summary and Source: Guatemala's Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026 (published July 6, 2026) secured it the 10% tier. Classification is Yes and has never been in doubt: the instrument is formally published by the competent authority, which the standing policy treats as enactment even before effectiveness. THE LONGEST-RUNNING OPEN QUESTION IN THIS TRACKER -- the entry-into-force date -- IS NOW RESOLVED, AND CONFIRMED GOVERNMENT-SIDE. Prensa Libre, August 18, 2026 (18:24h, Rosa Maria Bolanos), retrieved and read directly this run, reports: "El 17 de agosto del 2026 entro en vigencia el Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026, que prohibe en Guatemala las importaciones de bienes producidos mediante trabajo forzoso y obligatorio." It explains that the acuerdo was issued by the Ministerio de Economia (Mineco) jointly with the Ministerio de Trabajo y Prevision Social (Mintrab) and "establece que entra en vigencia 30 dias habiles despues de ser publicado en el diario oficial el 6 de julio ultimo," and -- decisively -- "AMBOS MINISTERIOS CONFIRMARON LA FECHA." That is confirmation from both competent ministries, far stronger than the outlet-characterisation evidence previously available, and it settles the 30-dias-HABILES reading against the 30-calendar-day reading. It also vindicates the AUGUST 16 CORRECTION recorded here, which reversed this row's August 12 framing: on August 12 this row had said the weight of evidence favoured a 30-CALENDAR-day count (~August 5, already in force), resting on the Diario de Centro America's parenthetical gloss of vigencia as "30 dias posteriores a la publicacion" with no "habiles" qualifier. That over-weighted a parenthetical; La Hora's same-day July 6 report ("la vigencia del Acuerdo sera efectiva dentro de 30 dias HABILES a partir de este 6 de julio") was the basis for the reversal, and 30 business days from July 6 lands exactly on Monday August 17, 2026. NEXT DEADLINE, NOW HARD-DATED: Mintrab has 90 dias calendario from entry into force to prepare and publish the Listado Oficial of foreign companies linked to forced labour, "plazo que, segun esa institucion, se cumple el 15 DE NOVIEMBRE proximo," and the publication must be made on the Mineco and Mintrab websites; to compile it Mintrab may use information obtained through diplomatic channels and other international sources. Economy Minister Gabriela Garcia said on Tuesday August 18 that Mintrab has asked the Ministerio de Relaciones Exteriores (Minex) to request the list of companies through diplomatic channels. Article 4 of the acuerdo carries the prohibition itself: "Se prohibe la importacion de bienes extranjeros extraidos, producidos o manufacturados total o parcialmente mediante trabajo forzoso u obligatorio." NEW THIS RUN, retrieved and read directly: a further Prensa Libre report ("Importaciones en Guatemala: expertos advierten riesgos por acuerdo sobre trabajo forzoso") sets out the implementation mechanics and the criticism of them. Mintrab is to compile the Listado Oficial by requesting information "por conducto diplomatico," updating it annually or when circumstances change, and MINECO is the body that transmits the list to the customs authority for the corresponding controls -- so SAT acts only once it receives the list, and no SAT implementing circular has been published. Ruben Morales, a former Economy Minister and foreign-trade specialist, and the other experts interviewed say the acuerdo's provisions are very broad, that it sets out no methodology for identifying goods linked to forced labour and provides for no independent Guatemalan investigation, leaving it dependent on foreign lists, and that it requires coordination between Mineco, Mintrab and SAT that is not clearly specified. These are implementation risks, not classification questions: the instrument is enacted and in force. Source: Prensa Libre, August 18 and August 2026; La Hora, July 6, 2026; Diario de Centro America (official gazette outlet), July 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026, published July 6, 2026, article 4 prohibiting importation of goods produced wholly or partly with forced or compulsory labour regardless of origin; ENTRY INTO FORCE CONFIRMED as MONDAY AUGUST 17, 2026 -- Prensa Libre, August 18, 2026 reports the acuerdo "entro en vigencia" that day on the 30-dias-habiles count and states that both competent ministries, Mineco and Mintrab, confirmed the date, which settles the question and vindicates this row's August 16 correction of its August 12 calendar-day framing. Mintrab's company-specific Listado Oficial is due 90 calendar days after vigencia, a deadline Mintrab itself puts at NOVEMBER 15, 2026, for publication on the Mineco and Mintrab websites; Economy Minister Gabriela Garcia said on August 18 that Mintrab has asked Minex to request the company list through diplomatic channels)

Summary and Source: Guyana's Ministry of Labour (represented by Sharon Roopchand-Edwards) testified at the July 7 USTR hearing, stating Guyana is "not aware of evidence" that forced-labor goods are made in, imported into, or exported from Guyana, citing constitutional protections, the Combating of Trafficking in Persons Act, ILO Convention 29/105 ratification, and Customs Act authority to block goods with credible evidence of forced labor; Guyana urged reconsideration of the proposed tariff and noted ongoing bilateral trade-agreement talks with the US. Source: Official USTR hearing transcript, Day 1, July 7, 2026. RTA-SEARCH RESULT WORTH RECORDING, August 15, 2026: a new US-Guyana bilateral instrument signed on August 11, 2026 was checked because the standing methodology requires following up any US bilateral deal regardless of headline framing. It is a defence/security arrangement -- a Guyana Defence Force / State Department liaison-officer memorandum -- not a trade agreement, and it carries no forced-labour or import-prohibition clause. It therefore does NOT place Guyana on the RTA-commitment watchlist. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 12.5% for Guyana, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No

Summary and Source: Honduras testified at the July 7 USTR hearing (Melvin Redondo, Presidential Office of Foreign Trade), announcing an executive decree creating an express prohibition on importing forced-labour-made goods, and requested a 10% "bridge rate." The Council of Ministers approved the decree on the night of July 16, 2026; it was published the next day as Decreto Ejecutivo No. PCM-014-2026 in La Gaceta No. 37,196 (July 17, 2026), citing ILO Conventions 29/105 and CAFTA-DR obligations. Article 4 prohibits importing goods produced wholly or partly with forced/compulsory labour, effective on publication, and Article 7 directs Customs to build the prohibited-goods list into its risk-management system, with intercepted goods facing re-export or destruction at importer cost. THE IMPLEMENTING LIST HAS NOW BEEN PUBLISHED, AND THIS ROW CORRECTS A SUSTAINED ERROR OF ITS OWN. Acuerdo Ministerial No. SETRASS-527-2026 -- "Regulacion para la implementacion del Decreto Ejecutivo PCM-014-2026 y aprobacion de la Lista de Mercancias con Prohibicion de Importacion, Primera Edicion 2026" -- was published as item 1 of La Gaceta Edition No. 37,226 of AUGUST 21, 2026, signed by Labour Secretary Fernando Puerto Castro. I read the full text directly. Article 32 puts the Acuerdo in force on the day of publication; Article 28 approves the Annex I list "integrada por seis registros"; and Article 29 defers the prohibition itself, so it "empezara a implementarse treinta dias calendario despues de la publicacion" -- i.e. ENFORCEMENT BEGINS SEPTEMBER 20, 2026. HOW THE LIST WAS BUILT, which is the substantively interesting part: the Permanent Technical Commission reported on August 14 that ILO, UN Special Rapporteur, Walk Free and US Department of Labor reports establish forced-labour practices in given countries or sectors but do NOT identify a specific producer or supply chain, so listing countries or regions from them would assume all their goods are tainted and create discrimination and trade barriers contrary to Article 6 of the decree. The Commission therefore built the First Edition EXCLUSIVELY from homologated US CBP Final Determinations (Findings), expressly excluding Withhold Release Orders as resting only on reasonable suspicion. It also declined to adopt the Xinjiang (UFLPA) entity list, reasoning that it was issued by an authority other than the customs authority and so is not shown to be equivalent under Article 3(e) -- left open for later editions. Article 14 forbids listings by tariff chapter, sector, country or region without an identified producer, and goods from prison establishments require extra analysis against the ILO C29 Article 2(2)(c) penal-labour exception. The six Annex I registros are five Chinese producers plus one fishing vessel: the Da Wang (operated by Yong Feng Fishery Ltd, Vanuatu-Taiwan, 87 FR 4634); Inner Mongolia Hengzheng Group Baoanzhao Agriculture, Industry and Trade (stevia extracts, 85 FR 66574); Tianjin Malleable Iron Factory a.k.a. Tianjin No. 2 prison (malleable iron pipe fittings, 61 FR 17956); Qinghai Hide & Garment Factory (sheepskins and leather); and two further Chinese producers. HS references are indicative only until Honduran Customs fixes the exact CAI classification under Article 15. The Honduran Chamber of Commerce and Industry (CCIT) has been warning importers that non-compliance could see goods blocked at the border. Source: Official USTR hearing transcript, Day 1, July 7, 2026; La Gaceta No. 37,196 of July 17, 2026 and No. 37,226 of August 21, 2026, both read directly via leyes.hn; Hondudiario and Proceso Digital, August 2026. USTR's final determination of July 23, 2026 confirmed a 10% tariff for Honduras.

Summary and Source: Japan submitted a written comment citing its July 2025 bilateral trade agreement with the US and asking for "appropriate actions" (implicit request for tariff relief); Japan did not testify live at the July 7-9 hearings. NEW CONTEXT THIS RUN, not enough to change the classification: an LDP lawmaker has floated drafting a Japanese UFLPA-style forced-labour import law, and Human Rights Watch has publicly urged Japan to adopt such a regulation. Both are proposals and advocacy -- no bill has been tabled in the Diet -- so Japan stays No under the standing policy, which requires at least a formally tabled or published measure for Partial. Source: International Economic Law and Policy Blog, July 2026; Human Rights Watch, February 2026. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 12.5% (net of MFN) for Japan, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. OPEN QUESTION RAISED THIS RUN, from the primary text and NOT acted on: the companion Presidential Document (Federal Register doc 2026-15274), which I retrieved and read directly, states that "for goods of the European Union, Japan, Korea, Switzerland, or Taiwan, section 301 tariffs that are the net of Most-Favored Nation (MFN) tariffs would be consistent with their respective Agreements on Reciprocal Trade or similar arrangements and would be appropriate to encourage these economies to fulfill commitments regarding forced labor imports." That sentence groups this economy with Taiwan, whose Partial classification rests precisely on an RTA forced-labour commitment, and its phrase "commitments regarding forced labor imports" could be read as implying one exists here too. It is NOT being treated as establishing one: the sentence is about how the tariff is calculated (netting against MFN) and about encouragement, the tariff outcome here is the 12.5% top-up rather than the 10% tier given to commitment economies, and no agreement text containing a forced-labour import-prohibition clause has been located. SETTLED THIS RUN, AND THE ANSWER IS NO. The only US-Japan instrument in force is the 2025 framework agreement announced July 22, 2025 and implemented by Executive Order 14345 of September 4, 2025 with Federal Register notices 2025-17389 and 2025-17908. Its substantive terms cover a 15% baseline tariff, sectoral carve-outs for autos, aerospace, pharmaceuticals and natural resources, Japanese purchase commitments on agricultural goods, energy and aircraft, an investment facility, and recognition of US auto standards -- and contain NO forced-labour, Section 307 or import-prohibition clause. No separate 2026 US-Japan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade exists, and Japan does not appear among the economies whose ARTs carry forced-labour commitments. The Presidential Document's "commitments regarding forced labor imports" phrasing is therefore encouraging or aspirational language in Japan's case, not a reference to an existing treaty clause. Japan stays No, and this question should not be reopened without new evidence of an actual instrument. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026; Federal Register doc 2026-15274 (primary text).
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No

THAT POSITION CHANGED DECISIVELY ON SEPTEMBER 13, AND IT IS NOW A POSITIVE REFUTATION RATHER THAN AN ABSENCE OF CONFIRMATION. The route in came from an unexpected direction: the US-Malaysia agreement was found on September 12 to place its forced-labour obligation at Article 2.9(1) and its entry-into-force mechanism in a separate article requiring an exchange of written notifications plus 60 days, which suggested these reciprocal-trade agreements share a template and that the Jordan text would have an equivalent. It does. I fetched the agreement text published on whitehouse.gov and its entry-into-force provision -- returned by the fetch as Article 6.6(2), and that NUMBER is held loosely because my query had suggested Malaysia's 7.2 and may have influenced it, though the mechanism itself was returned identically by two independent retrievals -- reads: "This Agreement shall enter into force 60 days after the date on which the Parties have notified each other in writing of the completion of their respective applicable internal procedures required for the entry into force of this Agreement." THE AGREEMENT WAS SIGNED ON JULY 21, 2026. Sixty days from signature is roughly September 19, and the sixty days do not even begin until both parties have exchanged written notifications, which no source shows has happened. An entry into force on AUGUST 1, 2026 -- eleven days after signature -- is therefore ARITHMETICALLY IMPOSSIBLE under the treaty's own terms, no matter how many outlets repeat it. The claim is not merely unverified now; it is inconsistent with the primary text, and it is rejected on that basis. A LIKELY SOURCE OF THE ERROR was also identified: an Arabic search returns the older US-Jordan Free Trade Agreement, which genuinely "دخلت حيز النفاذ في 17 كانون الأول 2001", so outlets may be transposing entry-into-force language from the 1990s FTA onto the new agreement. The text of that commitment was also confirmed directly: "Jordan shall, within five years of entry into force of this agreement, prohibit the importation of goods mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part by forced or compulsory labor", together with an obligation to recognise US Section 307 entity determinations and presumptively bar those companies' goods. Cinco de ellas corresponden a procedimientos de oficio enfocados en empresas del sector textil con origen en China", and "La sexta investigacion derivo de una peticion formal presentada por un tercero en noviembre del ano pasado sobre la fabricacion de productos de acero provenientes de la India". The single past-tense clause remains uncorroborated anywhere outside the Yahoo carry, and eleconomista.com.mx has now defeated three separate attempts across three days, with the search tool returning no hits on that domain for the phrase at all. So the two carries of one story disagree with each other, which is the likeliest explanation of the whole puzzle: a single ambiguous or re-edited original. Searching the exact phrase "se puso en marcha" restricted to eleconomista.com.mx returns ZERO hits, archive.org holds no snapshot of any relevant El Economista URL, and no MSN, Terra or Infobae carry exists. That domain has now defeated more than eight attempts across four days. SEPTEMBER 26 PRODUCES THE MOST LIKELY EXPLANATION OF THE WHOLE PUZZLE, AND IT IS THAT THE SOURCE TEXT MOVED UNDER US. The Yahoo carry was re-fetched at its exact URL (es-us.noticias.yahoo.com/mexico-alista-programa-piloto-trabajo-215920233.html) and it now reads "ALISTA" -- the preparatory verb -- and the past-tense clause "se puso en marcha un programa piloto" WAS NOT REPRODUCED ON THIS FETCH. The URL slug itself contains "alista". So the single piece of evidence for a launched pilot no longer appears at the address it came from, which points to a re-edited or mis-summarised original rather than to a real change of status. TWO FURTHER CHECKS CAME BACK EMPTY IN THE PLACE A REAL LAUNCH WOULD SHOW: a dof.gob.mx search found NO September 2026 acuerdo establishing a five-sector pilot, only the 2023 instrument's own entry, and gob.mx/stps/prensa carries only the 2023 instrument's original entry-into-force release, "Entra en vigor el Acuerdo para prohibir la importacion de mercancias producidas con trabajo forzoso", which is not a 2026 item. THE CLAIM IS NOW TREATED AS WITHDRAWN RATHER THAN MERELY UNADOPTED, the balance of evidence favours "prepared", and the row rests where it always did, on the enacted 2023 instrument.)

Summary and Source: Nicaragua enacted Ley No. 1280 (published in La Gaceta, April 9, 2026), adding Article 16 Bis to the customs self-clearance law (Ley No. 265), requiring importers, free-zone operators, and temporary-admission regimes to submit a sworn declaration that goods were not produced wholly or partly with forced labor, per an official format set by Customs Directorate Circular CT-027-2026; customs (DGA) may demand supply-chain traceability documentation and refer falsification for prosecution. Source: EY tax alert; Garcia & Bodan law firm summary, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (Ley No. 1280, April 9, 2026, adds Article 16 Bis to Ley No. 265 requiring a sworn no-forced-labor declaration for imports, with customs authority to investigate/penalize falsification; a declaration-and-investigation regime, not an outright import prohibition. Detail added September 4, which reinforces rather than changes the classification: practical application of Article 16 Bis is reported to remain pending the administrative provisions that the DGA and MIFIC must still issue to operationalise it, so the regime is enacted but not yet fully operative. A NEW CONFUSABLE LOGGED September 10, alongside the Dominican Decreto 502-26 that has been caught in Nicaragua searches five times: an article headlined "Hoy entra en vigencia" about a forced-labour import DECLARATION requirement, dated June 1, 2026, concerns EL SALVADOR, not Nicaragua. ONE PIECE OF GENUINE NEW CONTEXT ON SEPTEMBER 14: Ley No. 1280 was not a standalone measure but part of a package of three laws adopted together, Leyes 1278, 1279 and 1280, which is worth knowing because it suggests the forced-labour declaration requirement was folded into a broader legislative tidy-up rather than adopted as a targeted response to the Section 301 action. No September update on operative status and no new DGA or MIFIC implementing rules were found)

Summary and Source: Norway's government decided on July 21, 2026 to ban the import, export and sale of goods made with forced labour by incorporating EU Regulation 2024/3015 into the EEA Agreement, with Minister Cecilie Myrseth quoted: "Tvangsarbeid er selvfolgelig forbudt i Norge i dag, og gjennom dette regelverket innforer vi ogsa et forbud mot import av varer fremstilt ved tvangsarbeid." The regulation is marked "(Text with EEA relevance)," which is the basis for incorporation, and implementation is due no later than December 14, 2027. Re-checked in Norwegian on August 19, 2026 against both regjeringen.no and stortinget.no: regjeringen.no now states explicitly that "the necessary legislative work to implement the regulation in Norwegian law is underway" -- a small but genuine advance on the July 21 announcement -- but no Prop. til Stortinget has been tabled and no horing specific to this incorporation has appeared. The stortinget.no case search still returns only historical 2023-24 horing records on the EU regulation's Council position and the unrelated March 2026 Prop. 80 L on exploitation of foreign workers. Note regjeringen.no intermittently blocks automated fetch (403); this run the content was reachable via search cache. So this remains a formal government decision with no domestic implementing instrument enacted, which is Partial under the standing policy. FALSE-CLAIM GUARD, now traced to source: a claim that Norway has requested WTO dispute consultations over the US tariff has surfaced on several runs and has never been corroborated; this run it was pinned down -- the regjeringen.no WTO consultation-request pages being cited (id2604315 and id2616344) are from the 2018 steel and aluminium dispute, not this action. The claim is NOT recorded and should not be asserted. NEW THIS RUN: Adresseavisen, August 19, 2026 reports a state secretary in the Norwegian Foreign Ministry saying after a meeting with US officials that the Americans are clear a prohibition in progress is insufficient -- it must be adopted and in force before tariff relief follows. That is a useful external confirmation of the distinction this tracker itself draws between a decision to legislate and an enacted instrument, and it underlines that Norway's Partial rests on a government decision with no Storting proposition yet tabled. Source: regjeringen.no, July 21, 2026; NRK and NTB/FriFagbevegelse, July 21-22, 2026; stortinget.no case search.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (government decision July 21, 2026 to ban import/export/sale of forced-labour goods via EEA incorporation of EU Reg. 2024/3015, in force no later than December 14, 2027; implementing legislative work stated by regjeringen.no to be "underway" as of August 19, 2026, but no Storting proposition tabled and no Norwegian implementing instrument enacted. NEGATIVE UPGRADED TO DOCUMENT LEVEL ON SEPTEMBER 7: rather than inferring from news silence, a pass fetched the Storting's own "Saker som ventes fra regjeringen" list -- the register of propositions the government is expected to bring -- and it contains NO entry for a forced-labour or tvangsarbeid proposition and none for incorporating EU Regulation 2024/3015. That is a check against the body that would receive the instrument, not merely an absence of reporting about it, and it is the first time this row's negative has been established that way. RECONFIRMED, NOT MERELY REPEATED, ON SEPTEMBER 8: the register was fetched again and still carries no forced-labour or tvangsarbeid item and nothing on Regulation 2024/3015. What it DOES carry is instructive as a control -- an EEA vareloven amendment implementing EU Regulation 2019/1020 on market surveillance and product conformity, and parliamentary-consent items for trade agreements with Ukraine, Malaysia and MERCOSUR. So the register is populated with exactly the kind of trade instrument that would list a forced-labour measure if one were coming, and it does not list one. THE FLAGGED SOURCING GAP IS CLOSED ON SEPTEMBER 11: this row had been resting on search snippets for several runs and was explicitly marked as owing a fresh Storting fetch. That fetch succeeded today -- the "Saker som ventes fra regjeringen" register was retrieved directly, on a URL variant that had 404ed on an earlier attempt, and it still carries NO tvangsarbeid or forced-labour proposition and no item for incorporating EU Regulation 2024/3015, while continuing to carry the EEA vareloven amendment and the Ukraine, Malaysia and MERCOSUR consent items that make it a working control. The negative is document-level and current, not inherited, and it was re-fetched again on September 12 with the same result -- a THIRD consecutive direct read of the same primary register returning no tvangsarbeid proposition and no Regulation 2024/3015 item, while the labour, child-welfare, finance, health, justice, climate, agriculture, trade and fisheries, transport and foreign-affairs entries continue to populate it. Three independent reads of a working control is about as strong as a negative of this kind can be made, and a FOURTH consecutive direct read on September 13 returned the same result, with the EOS-vareloven market-surveillance item still present as the control. This row is now among the best-evidenced negatives in the file and needs no further daily re-reading; a weekly check would serve. A FIFTH consecutive direct read on September 16 returned the same result, with the Malaysia, Ukraine and MERCOSUR consent items confirmed still present as the working control and no tvangsarbeid or 2024/3015 entry anywhere. Moving to weekly from here. THE SEPTEMBER 21 WEEKLY RE-READ DID NOT SUCCEED AND IS NOT COUNTED AS A SIXTH CLEAN CONFIRMATION: stortinget.no/no/Saker-og-publikasjoner/Saker/Saker-som-ventes-fra-regjeringen/ loaded, but the extraction returned only navigation and structural content, with the fetching pass stating plainly that the list of bebudede saker "is referenced but not detailed in the provided text". The working control -- the Malaysia, Ukraine and MERCOSUR consent items -- was therefore NOT reproduced, so this read neither confirms nor contradicts the five clean ones before it. A page that loads is not a page that was read. Supplementary search found no Norwegian reporting of a tvangsarbeid import ban since 21 July. SEPTEMBER 22 EXPLAINS BOTH FAILURES AND RETIRES THE TEST. The page was fetched directly here (HTTP 200, 67,807 bytes, 5,715 characters of extracted text) and it WAS read successfully -- the reason the control items are missing is that THE LIST IS EMPTY BY DESIGN AT THIS TIME OF YEAR. The page states its own cadence: "Listen over bebudede saker sendes fra regjeringen til Stortinget to ganger i aaret - i oktober og rundt 1. februar", and, decisively, "Listen toemmes paa sommeren i paavente av hoestsesjonen" -- the list is EMPTIED over the summer pending the autumn session. Its scope line still reads "i loepet av vaarsesjonen 2026", the spring session. So the Malaysia, Ukraine and MERCOSUR consent items are gone because the register was cleared, not because two consecutive reads failed, and the working control I specified CANNOT be reproduced in this period. That control was therefore an invalid test from the moment the summer clearance happened, and my own instruction to treat its absence as a failed read was wrong -- both passes reported honestly and were misled by the instruction, not careless. The rule survives in better form: a page that loads is not a page that was read, but an empty register is also not a failed read. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: this register cannot show a tvangsarbeid item until the new list arrives in OCTOBER, so there is nothing to check here until then and daily or weekly re-reads are pointless. Norway is parked until the October list, and the row stands on the five clean spring-session reads. No Norwegian reporting of a tvangsarbeid import ban since 21 July)

Summary and Source: Peru's forced-labour import-ban bill was formally submitted to Congress on July 2, 2026 with "very urgent" status requested and referred to the Foreign Trade and Economy committees on July 6, but was never taken up: the Foreign Trade Commission closed its 2025-2026 session without addressing it and the Permanent Commission's term ended July 15. On the Executive's parallel route, Foreign Trade and Tourism Minister Rogers Valencia said a forced-labour import/dealings prohibition would be folded into the government's request to Congress for delegated legislative powers ("facultades legislativas"). PRECISION CORRECTION this run: this row previously stated that the Council of Ministers did not approve that request at its August 5 session. That overstated the sourcing. Summary and Source: On July 24, 2026, the Philippines' Trade, Labor, and Finance departments signed a Joint Administrative Order (JAO) establishing an inter-agency committee (DTI chair, DOLE vice-chair, plus DOF, Bureau of Customs, BOI, PEZA) to receive, investigate, and act on forced-labor-import complaints under existing customs-law authority (RA 10863); Trade Secretary Cristina Roque called it a measure to protect "people and...fair competition." This is an enacted administrative order but functions as an investigation/enforcement mechanism referencing existing law rather than a standalone blanket import prohibition, so it is classified Partial rather than Yes. NEW this run: Philippine officials are lobbying Washington to cut the 12.5% tariff to 10%, citing the JAO as the qualifying measure; no change to the classification, which turns on the instrument, not on the tier sought. Source: Manila Times, BusinessWorld, July 23-24, 2026; USTR press release, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (Joint Administrative Order signed July 24, 2026, establishing an inter-agency forced-labor-import investigation/enforcement mechanism under existing customs law; not itself a standalone blanket import prohibition. Joey Salceda, would create a standalone statutory import prohibition with Bureau of Customs exclusion and forfeiture powers and would put the JAO mechanism on a statutory footing. Summary and Source: At the July 9 hearing, Lee Seung-heon (Minister-Counselor for Commercial Affairs, Korean Embassy in Washington) testified the proposed 12.5% tariff is "neither appropriate nor necessary," arguing Korea should receive more favorable treatment given its separate trade/investment agreement and US investment commitments; USTR reportedly asked Korea for a forced-labor enforcement plan. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 12.5% (net of MFN) for South Korea, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. OPEN QUESTION RAISED THIS RUN, from the primary text and NOT acted on: the companion Presidential Document (Federal Register doc 2026-15274), which I retrieved and read directly, states that "for goods of the European Union, Japan, Korea, Switzerland, or Taiwan, section 301 tariffs that are the net of Most-Favored Nation (MFN) tariffs would be consistent with their respective Agreements on Reciprocal Trade or similar arrangements and would be appropriate to encourage these economies to fulfill commitments regarding forced labor imports." That sentence groups this economy with Taiwan, whose Partial classification rests precisely on an RTA forced-labour commitment, and its phrase "commitments regarding forced labor imports" could be read as implying one exists here too. It is NOT being treated as establishing one: the sentence is about how the tariff is calculated (netting against MFN) and about encouragement, the tariff outcome here is the 12.5% top-up rather than the 10% tier given to commitment economies, and no agreement text containing a forced-labour import-prohibition clause has been located. SETTLED THIS RUN, AND THE ANSWER IS NO. No KORUS FTA or Agreement on Reciprocal Trade text containing a Section 307-style IMPORT-prohibition commitment could be located. The KORUS labour chapter carries general ILO-style commitments to eliminate forced labour within Korea's own territory, which is a different thing entirely and does not qualify under the standing policy, since that requires a commitment targeting IMPORTS. Korean-language sources (VOA Korea, Sedaily) confirm Korea was placed among the economies USTR found to have NO legal forced-labour import prohibition, with the Sinan salt-farm case cited specifically, and USTR's own fact sheet listing the trading partners that gave RTA forced-labour commitments does not name Korea. The Presidential Document's "commitments regarding forced labor imports" phrasing is therefore about tariff netting and encouragement, not an existing clause. Korea stays No, and this question should not be reopened without new evidence of an actual instrument. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026; Federal Register doc 2026-15274 (primary text).
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No

New this run: Switzerland concluded a broader US trade agreement lowering its general tariff to about 15% in exchange for roughly $200bn of US investment through 2028. Checked specifically for a forced-labour or Section 307 clause per the Jordan precedent -- this is a general tariff-and-investment deal with no forced-labour import-prohibition commitment found, so it does not place Switzerland on the RTA-commitment watchlist. CLARIFIED AUGUST 13, 2026: the underlying November 2025 US-Switzerland-Liechtenstein instrument is a NON-BINDING joint framework statement / letter of intent, not a signed agreement; it references cooperation on forced-labour issues in general terms but contains no import-prohibition clause, and no final signed bilateral agreement text exists. So there is no treaty-level commitment capable of putting Switzerland on the watchlist even on the Jordan reading. OPEN QUESTION RAISED THIS RUN, from the primary text and NOT acted on: the companion Presidential Document (Federal Register doc 2026-15274), which I retrieved and read directly, states that "for goods of the European Union, Japan, Korea, Switzerland, or Taiwan, section 301 tariffs that are the net of Most-Favored Nation (MFN) tariffs would be consistent with their respective Agreements on Reciprocal Trade or similar arrangements and would be appropriate to encourage these economies to fulfill commitments regarding forced labor imports." That sentence groups this economy with Taiwan, whose Partial classification rests precisely on an RTA forced-labour commitment, and its phrase "commitments regarding forced labor imports" could be read as implying one exists here too. It is NOT being treated as establishing one: the sentence is about how the tariff is calculated (netting against MFN) and about encouragement, the tariff outcome here is the 12.5% top-up rather than the 10% tier given to commitment economies, and no agreement text containing a forced-labour import-prohibition clause has been located. SETTLED THIS RUN, AND THE ANSWER IS NO. No signed US-Switzerland agreement has materialised since the November 2025 instrument, which remains the "Joint Statement on a Framework for a United States-Switzerland-Liechtenstein Agreement on Fair, Balanced, and Reciprocal Trade" -- a non-binding framework, not a treaty. No fact sheet, joint statement or agreement text on ustr.gov, whitehouse.gov, seco.admin.ch or admin.ch contains language committing Switzerland to prohibit forced-labour imports. SECO's own July 2026 statements instead argue that Switzerland's existing constitutional, civil and criminal framework is "at least equivalent" to an import ban -- which is Switzerland's argument for why it should not need one, and the opposite of a commitment to adopt one. A negotiation reported as concluded on 20 August 2026 was checked and belongs to Switzerland-CHINA free-trade optimisation talks, not the United States. Switzerland stays No, and this question should not be reopened without new evidence of an actual signed instrument. A GERMAN-LANGUAGE PASS ON SEPTEMBER 13 PRODUCED SOMETHING BETTER THAN THE USUAL SILENCE, and it is worth recording because most negatives in this file are absences: the NZZ carries a piece headlined "Warum die Schweizer Wirtschaft kein Importverbot fuer Gueter aus Zwangsarbeit will" -- why Swiss business does NOT want an import ban on goods from forced labour. That is affirmative evidence of domestic opposition to the measure, which is a stronger foundation for a negative than the absence of reporting, and it makes a near-term Swiss ban materially less likely rather than merely unevidenced. SECO talks toward a permanent arrangement with the United States continue with no signed treaty. Source: swissinfo.ch, July 24, 2026; Barchart/Reuters, July 2026; Federal Register doc 2026-15274 (primary text); Neue Zuercher Zeitung, September 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (no legislation explicitly prohibiting forced-labour imports; a narrow due-diligence draft law covering only large companies does not amount to an import prohibition)

Summary and Source: Taiwan's 10%-tier eligibility rests on its February 12, 2026 US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, under which Taiwan committed to prohibit forced-labor-produced imports. INSTRUMENT NOW ISSUED: on July 30, 2026 the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Ministry of Labor jointly issued the "Operating Guidelines for Restricting the Import of Forced Labor Goods" and a companion "Review Committee Establishment Guidelines," under Article 11 of the Foreign Trade Act -- the administrative instrument previously recorded here as forthcoming. A 12-member review committee co-chaired by the MOEA and MOL ministers must decide within 30 days of receiving a forced-labour referral, after which the competent authority publishes a notice restricting or lifting the import restriction, with Customs and the Finance Ministry notifying importers to return or destroy listed goods. Column 6 accordingly upgraded to Taiwan's own Ministry of Labor announcement. Classification remains Partial on the same reasoning applied to the Philippines' Joint Administrative Order: this is an enforcement regime under existing statutory authority, not a standalone enacted import prohibition, and no Legislative Yuan bill has been tabled (the separate Employment Service Act amendments address labour brokerage, not imports). SEQUENCE CLARIFIED this run: the Executive Yuan approved the mechanism on July 29, 2026 and MOEA/MOL formally announced it the following day, July 30 -- the date this row already carried. Also new: Amnesty International Taiwan is publicly pressing the government to LEGISLATE the labour provisions of the US-Taiwan agreement rather than continue relying on administrative guidelines, which is the step that would move Taiwan from Partial to Yes; no Legislative Yuan bill has been tabled. Source: Public Television Service (PTS) and Executive Yuan Section 301 portal, July 29-30, 2026; Amnesty International Taiwan; Ministry of Labor (Taiwan, official), July 30, 2026; Newtalk and Taipei Times, July 30-31, 2026; USTR fact sheet, February 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (US-Taiwan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, February 12, 2026 treaty commitment, now implemented through MOEA/MOL Operating Guidelines and a Review Committee issued July 30, 2026 under Foreign Trade Act Art. 11; still an administrative regime under existing authority -- no statutory import prohibition enacted and no Legislative Yuan bill tabled. Re-confirmed September 4, with the mechanism described more precisely: MOEA and the Ministry of Labor operate a twelve-member cross-agency review committee under the existing Foreign Trade Act, and Taiwanese reporting states plainly that Taiwan "has not yet fully completed legislation prohibiting the import of goods produced through forced labor." A separate Employment Service Act amendment on document and property withholding is pending in the Legislative Yuan but is NOT an import-ban bill and should not be mistaken for one. A GENUINE CHINESE-LANGUAGE LEGISLATIVE YUAN SEARCH WAS RUN ON SEPTEMBER 12, the previous run's having returned only English coverage: it found no import-ban bill before the Legislative Yuan, and found Amnesty International Taiwan still arguing that "台灣政府應立法落實" -- the government SHOULD legislate to implement the agreement -- which is advocacy for a bill that does not exist and is itself evidence the legislative step has not been taken. The administrative MOEA and MOL mechanism of July 29-30 remains the whole of Taiwan's domestic action. SEPTEMBER 14 ADDS NOTHING AND THE REASON IS RECORDED RATHER THAN CONCEALED: the research pass disclosed that it ran a Chinese-language query about THAILAND'S labour situation by mistake instead of a Legislative Yuan query about Taiwan, so it returned Radio Taiwan International coverage of Thai tariffs and nothing about ly.gov.tw. Neither did I re-run it. That day was therefore unverified. SEPTEMBER 15 PARTLY REPAIRS IT: a corrected Chinese-language query was run and found no import-ban bill before the Legislative Yuan, with Amnesty International Taiwan still publishing its 台灣政府應立法落實 advocacy -- an argument that the government SHOULD legislate, which continues to be evidence that it has not. But the pass disclosed that this was a general web search rather than a site-level query against ly.gov.tw, so the legislature's own database had not been consulted. THAT GAP IS NOW CLOSED, September 16, after being owed for three runs: a site-level Chinese query against ly.gov.tw was finally run and returned only the Legislative Yuan's own Legal Affairs Bureau research papers -- among them "我國強迫勞動相關議題之研析", an analysis of forced-labour issues, and a study of the EU forced-labour regulation. Research briefs are not bills. So the legislature's own site confirms there is no tabled import-ban bill, and the negative is now first-hand rather than inferred from news silence. It is also quietly telling that the Legislative Yuan's research service is studying the EU regulation: that is what preparatory work looks like before a bill exists, not a bill. SEPTEMBER 22 RECORDS THE AGREEMENT'S ARTICLE NUMBER AND WARNS AGAINST THE OBVIOUS CONFLATION: udn.com cites the forced-labour import-prohibition commitment as sitting at "臺美對等貿易協定" Article 3.9, NOT at Article 2.9 where the US-Malaysia and US-Jordan agreements both place it. The template that made those two tractable therefore does NOT carry across to Taiwan, and anyone checking Article 2.9 of the Taiwan text would draw a false negative. A Chinese-language pass found Executive Yuan and PTS coverage of the administrative mechanism and continuing Amnesty Taiwan advocacy that "台灣政府應立法落實", and NO tabled Legislative Yuan bill, which is what would move this row. SEPTEMBER 23 ATTEMPTED THE SITE-LEVEL ly.gov.tw QUERY THAT WAS OWED AND IT FAILED AS A TOOLING FAILURE, NOT AS A NEGATIVE: the direct request died with a proxy CONNECT-tunnel error (502), so no page was ever served and nothing was read. Summary and Source: Thailand's Cabinet (June 23, 2026) approved the "Committee on Determining Standards for Imported Goods at Risk of Forced Labour or Services," chaired by the Labour Minister, to set Watchlist/Blacklist/Risk List criteria under Section 5 of the Export and Import of Goods Act B.E. 2522 (1979); re-checked August 13, 2026 against the Royal Gazette (ratchakitcha.soc.go.th) and Thai-language sources, no proclamation, watchlist or blacklist has been published. NEW this run, and it does NOT change the classification: Thai reporting indicates the Labour Ministry is DRAFTING a bill for eventual submission to parliament, and Commerce Minister Suphajee has said the US undervalues Thailand's efforts. Re-confirmed August 14 via Thai-language reporting (Prachatai, Kaohoon, Nation Thailand, prd.go.th) that the bill remains at the DRAFTING stage and has not been submitted to parliament. FURTHER NEW THIS RUN, also not enough to move the classification: the Prime Minister has directed six ministries, led by the Labour Ministry, to prepare enforcement and traceability measures. That is an executive directive to prepare, not an enacted or tabled instrument, so it stays on the No side of the line. A measure being drafted is not a measure formally tabled or published, so it falls short of the Partial threshold; if the bill is actually tabled, Thailand moves to Partial. NEW THIS RUN: the Cabinet-established Committee on Determining Standards for Imported Goods at Risk of Forced Labour or Services held its FIRST meeting on August 14, 2026, per the Ministry of Labour's own announcement (mol.go.th), agreeing to establish subcommittees and to draft screening standards and guidelines. That is the committee beginning to organise itself, not an instrument: no Royal Gazette proclamation, watchlist or blacklist has issued from it, so Thailand stays No. It does show the Section 5 route is live rather than dormant, and it is the first concrete activity from this committee since its June 23 creation. Thailand held technical talks with USTR in May. Source: Mahanakorn Partners Group / Bloomberg Tax, June 2026. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 12.5% for Thailand, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (committee established under existing trade law; no Royal Gazette proclamation, watchlist or blacklist published as of August 21, 2026, though the committee held its first meeting on August 14, 2026 and agreed to form subcommittees and draft screening standards; the Labour Ministry's bill is still only being drafted, not tabled, and a new PM directive to six ministries to prepare enforcement measures remains at the directive stage. Routing clarified September 1, 2026: the Cabinet decision is being channelled to the Department of Foreign Trade to issue a Royal Gazette notice under Section 5 of the Export and Import Act -- that notice, if it appears, is the specific instrument that would move this row, and it has not appeared. RECLASSIFICATION TO PARTIAL PROPOSED THIS RUN, CONSIDERED SERIOUSLY, AND REJECTED ON THE PRIMARY TEXT. A research pass argued the June 2026 Cabinet decision satisfies the standing policy's Partial limb (iv), "a formal government decision with instrument pending." That is a fair question, so I read the Thai government's own account -- the Public Relations Department release -- rather than the secondary summaries. It says the Cabinet "มีมติเห็นชอบตามที่กระทรวงแรงงานเสนอ ในการกำหนดหลักเกณฑ์สินค้านำเข้าที่มีความเสี่ยงการใช้แรงงานบังคับ" and approved TWO things: acknowledging the investigation findings, and approving the ESTABLISHMENT of a "คณะกรรมการกำหนดมาตรฐานสินค้านำเข้าที่มีความเสี่ยงจากการบังคับใช้แรงงานหรือบริการ" chaired by the Labour Minister. That committee's function is to set criteria and document-verification standards and to PROPOSE a Watchlist/Blacklist/Risk List back TO THE CABINET ("เสนอบัญชีรายชื่อเสี่ยง ... ต่อ ครม."). So the decision creates a BODY THAT WILL LATER PROPOSE measures; it is not itself a decision to adopt a measure with an instrument merely awaiting publication. No list has been proposed, let alone approved or gazetted, and the phrase "ห้ามนำเข้า" (prohibit import) appears ZERO times in either account. That places Thailand alongside South Africa's announced intent to consult rather than alongside a pending instrument, so it stays No. This is a considered judgment on a genuinely arguable point, not a brush-off: if the committee proposes a Risk List and the Cabinet approves it, or a Section 5 Royal Gazette notice issues, this row moves. A SECOND AND ENTIRELY DIFFERENT PATHWAY OPENED INTO VIEW ON SEPTEMBER 13 and is flagged as the live watch item for this row: Thailand-US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade negotiations are reported to be in their final stages, with Nation Thailand of September 8-10 reporting that every major issue has been settled and Thai Examiner of September 10 reporting that a call between Prime Minister Anutin and President Trump could finalise it. THIS MATTERS BECAUSE OF THE TEMPLATE FINDING made elsewhere in this file today: the US-Malaysia and US-Jordan reciprocal-trade agreements both carry a forced-labour import-prohibition commitment at Article 2.9(1), with an implementation deadline running from entry into force. If the Thai agreement follows the same template and is signed, Thailand would join the RTA-commitment watchlist and move from No to Partial on treaty grounds alone, without any domestic Thai measure. NOTHING IS ADOPTED YET AND THE ROW DOES NOT MOVE: no signed text and no fact sheet has been published, the reporting describes the tariff structure rather than a country-specific forced-labour clause, and this tracker does not classify on the basis of a negotiation reported to be nearly finished. The instruction to a future run is specific -- when a Thai agreement is announced, do not read the headline, fetch the text and look for an Article 2.9-equivalent. CHECKED ON SEPTEMBER 14 AND NOT YET SIGNED: Nation Thailand of September 8 quotes Deputy Prime Minister and Commerce Minister Suphajee saying talks are down to "final wording" and expected to conclude within about a week, and Thai Examiner of September 10 describes the deal as ready to be finalised by an Anutin-Trump call. Searches of ustr.gov and whitehouse.gov surfaced nothing beyond the October 2025 framework joint statement, so THERE IS NO TEXT AND NO FACT SHEET TO CHECK and the Article 2.9 question cannot yet be answered -- which is stated plainly rather than filled in from the template. SEPTEMBER 15 RESOLVES THE IMMEDIATE QUESTION IN THE NEGATIVE, AND USEFULLY SO: the Anutin-Trump call that was expected to finalise the agreement HAS NOW TAKEN PLACE AND DID NOT CONCLUDE IT. Wire coverage reports that Thailand says tariff talks will CONTINUE after the call. So the agreement remains unsigned, there is still no text and no fact sheet on ustr.gov or whitehouse.gov, and the Article 2.9 question therefore still cannot be answered -- which is stated plainly rather than filled in from the Malaysia and Jordan template. This is the second consecutive run in which reporting described the deal as days away; that pattern is itself worth noting, because "final wording" has now persisted for a week. SEPTEMBER 17: still unsigned, and the timeline moved again rather than resolving. Bangkok Post carried "PM Anutin asks Trump for 'better' trade deal", and Nation Thailand now reports a further call PROPOSED for September 17 or 18 -- so the call this row recorded as having already happened and not concluded the agreement is to be followed by another. No signed text, no fact sheet on ustr.gov or whitehouse.gov beyond the October 2025 framework joint statement, and therefore still nothing to check for an Article 2.9-equivalent. SEPTEMBER 18 SHARPENS THE PATTERN RATHER THAN BREAKING IT: the further Anutin-Trump call proposed for 17 or 18 September had NOT occurred as of the 17 September reporting, which describes the prime minister as one who "may speak with" the president soon, and the Department of Trade Negotiations director-general Chotima Iemsawasdikul is quoted on 16 September saying there is "still no firm timetable for concluding the deal". So this is a fourth consecutive run in which an agreement has been days away, and the only official on the record says there is no timetable. No signed text and no fact sheet exists beyond the October 2025 framework joint statement, so the Article 2.9-equivalent question still cannot be answered. SEPTEMBER 19 -- A FIFTH CONSECUTIVE RUN OF IMMINENCE, AND THE GOALPOST HAS MOVED AGAIN, which is now the most informative thing about this row. The call proposed for 17-18 September had still not occurred as of 18 September reporting. Nation Thailand of that date states: "No official date has been confirmed for tariff and trade talks between Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and US President Donald Trump ahead of Anutin's September 21-27, 2026, visit to the United States", adding that the trip is primarily to attend the UN General Assembly and that "no official arrangements ... made for discussions with the US president on the sidelines". So the expectation has degraded in stages -- from an agreement at "final wording" in early September, to a specific finalising call, to an unscheduled possibility on the margins of a UN trip. Tracking that degradation is more useful than tracking each fresh claim of imminence. No signed text and no fact sheet exists beyond the October 2025 framework joint statement, so the Article 2.9-equivalent question still cannot be answered, and this row will not move on reporting of intent. A SIXTH CONSECUTIVE RUN, September 20: the call still has not happened and nothing has been signed. Anutin's US visit begins TOMORROW, 21 September, running to the 27th, and the reporting is explicit that it is primarily for the UN General Assembly with "no official arrangements ... made for discussions with the US president on the sidelines". SEPTEMBER 21 -- THE VISIT HAS NOW BEGUN AND THE POSITION HAS DEGRADED FURTHER RATHER THAN RESOLVED, a seventh consecutive run of imminence without signature. Nation Thailand of today, "Anutin cites one extra US tariff condition ahead of UN trip" (nationthailand.com/business/trade/40071264), reports that "No meeting with President Trump has been scheduled during Anutin's UN trip", with Anutin quoted as intending to "play it by ear". Two further quotes matter more than the scheduling: Anutin said "I had not asked for details of the additional US condition" -- so a NEW and unspecified US condition has entered the negotiation at this late stage -- and that "A draft tariff agreement would be sent to the leaders of both countries when the negotiations reached the appropriate stage", which places the process explicitly pre-signature and pre-text. The trajectory this row has tracked since early September is now complete: from an agreement at "final wording", to a finalising call, to an unscheduled possibility on the margins of a UN trip, to an extra condition the Thai side has not even read. SEPTEMBER 22 IS AN EIGHTH CONSECUTIVE RUN OF IMMINENCE WITHOUT SIGNATURE, checked in Thai as well as English across bangkokbiznews.com, thansettakij.com and prachachat.net and directly at ustr.gov and whitehouse.gov. Still no scheduled meeting, still no signed text, still nothing beyond the October 2025 framework joint statement. The additional US condition remains UNSPECIFIED by every source -- Anutin is relying on Commerce Minister Suphajee's assurance that it is resolvable, and no report describes its content, so it cannot be assessed against Article 2.9-equivalent language. A NEW FIGURE IS RECORDED WITH AN EXPLICIT WARNING NOT TO CONFLATE IT: Thai reporting now describes the Thai side targeting a 19% tariff outcome. That is a general tariff negotiating target and has NOTHING to do with the forced-labour question or with this file's 12.5% and 10% Section 301 tiers, and it must not be folded into either. SEPTEMBER 23 IS A NINTH CONSECUTIVE RUN OF IMMINENCE WITHOUT SIGNATURE, with day three of the visit gone and the position unchanged on all three questions: no meeting scheduled or held, the additional US condition still unreported in substance, and no signed text or fact sheet. USTR's own Thailand country page was fetched directly and its text contains "Reciprocal Trade" but ZERO occurrences of "forced labor" or "301 investigation", so the silence is now confirmed at the agency's own page rather than inferred from news. SEPTEMBER 24, DAY FOUR OF THE VISIT AND A TENTH CONSECUTIVE RUN OF IMMINENCE WITHOUT SIGNATURE. All three questions return the same answers: no meeting scheduled or held, no signed text or fact sheet at ustr.gov or whitehouse.gov, and the additional US condition still unreported in substance -- Thai Examiner of 21 September puts it plainly, "Anutin has not disclosed what the new American demand involves". A CONFUSABLE IS LOGGED THAT WOULD HAVE ANSWERED THE WRONG QUESTION: mgronline.com and sondhitalk of 17 September quote Anutin listing conditions Thailand has ALREADY fulfilled -- "ไปเก็บกู้ทุ่นระเบิด ไปถอนทหาร ดำเนินการปราบปรามสแกมเมอร์" -- UXO clearance, troop withdrawal and a scam-centre crackdown. Those belong to the OLDER Cambodia-border joint-statement condition set, not to the new unspecified US condition, and a pass looking for the missing content could easily have mistaken one for the other. SEPTEMBER 25, DAY FIVE OF SEVEN AND AN ELEVENTH CONSECUTIVE RUN OF IMMINENCE WITHOUT SIGNATURE. The visit ends on the 27th and all three questions still return nothing: no Trump-Anutin meeting reported as held or scheduled, the additional US condition's content unreported by every English and Thai source checked, and no signed text or fact sheet. USTR's own Thailand country page was fetched directly again and contains ZERO occurrences of "forced labor", referring only to the 2002 TIFA. Both standing warnings held this run: the 19% figure is a general tariff target unrelated to this file's 12.5% and 10% forced-labour tiers, and Anutin's list of conditions already met belongs to the older Cambodia-border joint statement. SEPTEMBER 26 ANSWERS THE QUESTION THE REPORTING NEVER DID, AND IT DOES SO BY ITINERARY RATHER THAN BY STATEMENT. Anutin's trip is now reported as New York for the UN through about 24 September, then LONDON on 25-26 September, then home to Thailand on the 27th. THERE IS NO WASHINGTON LEG AT ALL. So the "US visit" that eleven consecutive runs treated as the occasion for a possible signature never contained a bilateral meeting in its schedule, and the window closes in ABSENCE rather than in refusal -- no meeting held, none ever scheduled, the additional US condition's content still unreported by any English or Thai source, and no signed text or fact sheet at ustr.gov or whitehouse.gov. This is the twelfth and final run of this particular imminence cycle, and the lesson it leaves is the one this row has been applying throughout: reporting that an agreement is close is not evidence that it is close, and a trip described as a chance to sign is not a scheduled signing. Thailand stays No, and will not move on reporting of intent)

Summary and Source: The specific domestic instrument has now been located and verified directly: Trinidad and Tobago's Finance Act, 2026 (Act No. 16 of 2026), assented to on 25 June 2026 and published in Legal Supplement Part A to the Trinidad and Tobago Gazette, Vol. 65, No. 111, 29 June 2026, section 24 amends the Customs Act (Chap. 78:01) section 45(1) by inserting a new paragraph: "(w) all goods produced from forced labour as designated by the Minister with responsibility for trade". Section 45(1) is the Customs Act's list of prohibited/restricted imports, so this is a genuine, enacted, gazetted forced-labor import prohibition (designation-dependent -- the specific list of goods is left to the Minister with responsibility for trade to designate, similar in structure to several other economies' framework-style bans). This confirms and supersedes the prior entry's reliance on USTR's Federal Register final-action notice (which had stated, without naming the instrument, that Trinidad and Tobago "adopt[ed] a forced labor import prohibition subsequent to the publication of the June 5, 2026 FRN" -- the Finance Act's 25 June 2026 assent date fits neatly within that window). USTR's final action (July 23, 2026) placed Trinidad and Tobago in the 10% tariff tier on this basis. Source: Trinidad and Tobago e-Gazette (printery.gov.tt), Finance Act 2026 (Act No. 16 of 2026), 29 June 2026; USTR Federal Register final-action notice, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Finance Act, 2026, Act No. 16 of 2026, assented 25 June 2026, gazetted 29 June 2026, section 24 amends Customs Act Chap. 78:01 s.45(1) by adding paragraph (w) prohibiting the importation of goods produced from forced labour, as designated by the Minister with responsibility for trade -- a framework-style ban pending ministerial designation of the specific goods list. Re-checked September 6 after several runs of being carried forward without a fresh search: the SUBSTANCE is reconfirmed -- clause 24 amends the Customs Act to prohibit importing goods produced wholly or partly by forced labour "when designated by the Minister with responsibility for trade" -- but the specific subsection cite 45(1)(w) was NOT re-verified against the primary bill text this run, only the substance. The distinction is recorded rather than glossed. A CONTRADICTING CLAIM SURFACED ON SEPTEMBER 14 AND WAS REJECTED, with the reasoning recorded because the shape of it will recur: an AI-generated search summary asserted that Trinidad and Tobago is among "54 economies that have failed to impose" a forced-labour import ban, which would contradict this row entirely. It cites and quotes no primary source, it conflicts with the gazetted Finance Act 2026 text verified directly for this row, and it has the characteristic form of a synthesis reconstructing the original 46-economy tier list rather than reporting a finding. A generated summary that contradicts a primary text read directly loses to the primary text. Not adopted)

Summary and Source: USTR credited the UK with a "partial regime" (2023 Procurement Act forced-labour exclusions, 2025 Great British Energy Act provisions), securing the 10% tier. No government import-ban bill has been tabled: bills.parliament.uk shows only the Import of Products of Forced Labour from Xinjiang (Prohibition) Bill, a narrow private member's bill; the Joint Committee on Human Rights report and the Independent Anti-Slavery Commissioner's December 2025 "model legislative drafting" report are advisory; and the Employment Rights Act 2025 (Fair Work Agency) is domestic enforcement, not an import measure. The JCHR's "Forced Labour in UK Supply Chains" report is scheduled for debate in the House of Lords on September 4, 2026. A further scheduling detail added this run: the Immigration and Asylum Bill's Public Bill Committee sits for the first time on September 10, 2026 for line-by-line scrutiny. Neither date changes the classification, since that bill's forced-labour provisions are TISC disclosure duties rather than an import prohibition NEW this run: a formal Government Response to that report has now been published on publications.parliament.uk, reiterating that the government is "considering" the findings ahead of the Lords debate. A published government response to a select-committee report is still deliberative -- it is not a bill and creates no measure -- so it does not affect the classification, but it is the first formal written government reply in this sequence. Trade Minister Chris Bryant said on June 30, 2026 that government is still debating design and enforcement but hopes to legislate before this Parliament ends (~2029). Summary and Source: Vietnam's Government issued Decree No. 292/2026/ND-CP on July 22, 2026, implementing the Law on Foreign Trade Management; item 23 of its Appendix I prohibited-import list bans "products and goods extracted, produced, or manufactured wholly or partly through forced labor." Effective September 5, 2026 (45 days after issuance). Vietnam's Foreign Ministry separately rejected USTR's findings and reiterated that Vietnam "strictly prohibits all forms of forced labour." IMPLEMENTATION MECHANISM PINNED DOWN this run: per Article 5(2) of the decree, ministries and ministerial-level agencies are tasked with announcing the detailed HS-code-level goods lists built on Appendix I -- so the decree is self-executing as a prohibition but depends on those ministerial lists for operational scope. Re-checked in Vietnamese on September 26, 2026 -- the twenty-second day the decree has been in force: no ministerial HS-code list, no implementing circular (thong tu) and no General Department of Customs preparation notice has been published. WATCH ITEM NOW RESOLVED: yesterday's single-source claim that the forced-labour category is administered by the Ministry of Interior/Home Affairs (Bo Noi vu) rather than a trade ministry has been corroborated by multiple independent Vietnamese sources (luatvietnam.vn, congluan.vn, vietnam.vn) citing Appendix I of the decree directly ("nhom hang hoa nay do Bo Noi vu quan ly"). It is therefore adopted rather than merely flagged. This matters practically: it identifies which body must issue the Article 5(2) HS-code list, and it is an unusual assignment for an import-control category, so the list is not to be expected from the trade ministry. Note the decree predated USTR's July 23 final determination by one day yet Vietnam was still placed in the 12.5% tier. Source: Bao Chinh Phu (Vietnam Government Portal), July 22-23, 2026; Lao Dong; LuatVietnam and RBV, July-August 2026.
